title: The Islamic Republic
subtitle: 1979–today · Revolution, the Iran-Iraq War, and Decades of Confrontation

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Khomeini's founding, Khamenei's long tenure, and a rotating cast of presidents

entries.label: Ayatollah Khomeini — Founding the Islamic Republic
entries.hint: Returning from exile in February 1979 to a collapsing monarchy, Khomeini oversaw an April 1979 referendum establishing an Islamic Republic and a December 1979 constitution built around his own doctrine of velayat-e faqih (guardianship of the Islamic jurist) — creating a political system with an elected president and parliament operating under the ultimate authority of an unelected clerical Supreme Leader.
entries.note: Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Iran (1979), full text; 1979 referendum results as reported by the Iranian government.

entries.label: Ali Khamenei — Supreme Leader
entries.hint: Selected by the Assembly of Experts to succeed Khomeini within a day of his death in 1989, Ali Khamenei has held the position of Supreme Leader for over three and a half decades, making him — as of 2026 — the second-longest-serving head of state in modern Iranian history after Mohammad Reza Shah.
entries.note: Assembly of Experts selection announcement (June 1989); Iranian state media reporting on Khamenei's tenure, current as of 2026.

entries.label: The Early Presidents — Bani-Sadr to Rafsanjani
entries.hint: Abolhassan Bani-Sadr, Iran's first president, was impeached by parliament and fled the country in 1981 amid a power struggle with clerical authorities; Ali Khamenei then served as president himself from 1981 until his elevation to Supreme Leader in 1989, followed by Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani's two terms overseeing postwar economic reconstruction.
entries.note: Iranian parliamentary impeachment records (1981); Iranian presidential election results, 1981–1993.

entries.label: Khatami's Reformist Era
entries.hint: Mohammad Khatami won the presidency with a large majority on a platform of political and social liberalisation, expanding press freedom and civil society space for several years before conservative institutions — the judiciary, the Guardian Council, and security bodies outside his direct control — rolled back much of the reform agenda's practical scope by the end of his second term.
entries.note: Iranian presidential election results (1997, 2001); comparative assessment of press and civil-society space during the Khatami presidency.

entries.label: Ahmadinejad and the Disputed 2009 Election
entries.hint: Mahmoud Ahmadinejad's combative foreign-policy rhetoric and disputed 2009 re-election — which opposition candidates and their supporters rejected as fraudulent, triggering the largest street protests since the revolution — marked a period of sharpened international confrontation over the nuclear programme alongside serious internal political contestation over the election result itself.
entries.note: Iranian Interior Ministry's official 2009 election results; comparative international and opposition assessments disputing those results.

entries.label: Rouhani, Raisi, and the Present
entries.hint: Hassan Rouhani's presidency negotiated the 2015 nuclear agreement before its unilateral American withdrawal in 2018; Ebrahim Raisi, elected in 2021, died in a helicopter crash in May 2024; Masoud Pezeshkian was elected to succeed him in July 2024 and remains in office as of 2026.
entries.note: Iranian Interior Ministry election results, 2013–2024; Iranian government statements on Raisi's death and the 2024 election.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The hostage crisis, the Iran-Iraq War, and three decades of street protest

entries.label: The Iran Hostage Crisis
entries.hint: Iranian students seized the US embassy in Tehran in November 1979, holding 52 American diplomats and staff hostage for 444 days — the crisis dominated US-Iran relations for the following two years and severed formal diplomatic relations between the two countries that remain broken as of 2026.
entries.note: US State Department records on the hostage crisis; the hostages were released on 20 January 1981.

entries.label: The Iran-Iraq War
entries.hint: Saddam Hussein's 1980 invasion began eight years of war that included Iraqi chemical weapons use against Iranian forces and civilians and Iranian use of child and teenage volunteers in human-wave assaults — estimated total deaths on both sides range from roughly 500,000 to over a million depending on the source, a wide range reflecting the war's exceptionally poor casualty documentation.
entries.note: Comparative Iran-Iraq War casualty estimates from UN, academic and Iranian and Iraqi government sources, which vary substantially.

entries.label: The Green Movement
entries.hint: Mass protests following the disputed 2009 presidential election, organised partly through then-novel social media use, represented the largest sustained popular challenge to the Islamic Republic's political system since 1979 — a government crackdown that included documented arrests, deaths and allegations of custodial abuse ended the movement's street presence within several months, though its political effects persisted longer.
entries.note: Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International reporting on the 2009 post-election crackdown.

entries.label: The November 2019 Fuel Protests
entries.hint: A sudden government fuel price increase triggered nationwide protests met with a severe security crackdown and a near-total, multi-day internet shutdown that made independent documentation of events unusually difficult — Amnesty International's investigation documented over 300 deaths, while Iranian officials disputed the scale and framing of international estimates.
entries.note: Amnesty International, 'Trampling Humanity' report (2020), on the November 2019 protests; Iranian government statements disputing the reported casualty figures.

entries.label: The Woman, Life, Freedom Protests
entries.hint: Mahsa Jina Amini's death in the custody of Iran's morality police in September 2022, after her arrest for allegedly improper hijab, triggered months of nationwide protests under the slogan 'Woman, Life, Freedom' — United Nations investigators documented hundreds of deaths and thousands of arrests in the subsequent crackdown, findings the Iranian government has disputed.
entries.note: UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on the Islamic Republic of Iran, report (2024); Iranian government statements disputing the Mission's findings and mandate.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The 1979 constitution and the Guardian Council's power to vet candidates

entries.label: The Constitution and Velayat-e Faqih
entries.hint: The 1979 constitution created a hybrid system combining republican institutions — an elected president and parliament (Majlis) — with an unelected Supreme Leader holding ultimate authority over the judiciary, military and broad policy direction, formalising Khomeini's doctrine that clerical religious authority should hold final political sovereignty.
entries.note: Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Iran (1979, amended 1989), full text.

entries.label: The Guardian Council's Vetting Power
entries.hint: The twelve-member Guardian Council, half appointed directly by the Supreme Leader, screens all candidates for the presidency, parliament and the Assembly of Experts for ideological and religious suitability before they may stand for election — a vetting power that has excluded large numbers of reformist and other candidates in every election cycle since the system's founding.
entries.note: Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Iran, Articles 91–99, on the Guardian Council's composition and powers; comparative election-cycle candidate disqualification data.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: State Shiism's institutions, and the documented persecution of the Baha'i

entries.label: The Persecution of the Baha'i
entries.hint: Iran's Baha'i minority, whose faith the constitution does not recognise as a protected religion, has faced systematic exclusion from higher education and government employment, arbitrary detention, and periodic destruction of cemeteries and holy sites — treatment the UN Special Rapporteur on Iran has documented in successive reports as sustained, state-organised religious persecution.
entries.note: UN Special Rapporteur on the Situation of Human Rights in the Islamic Republic of Iran, successive annual reports; Baha'i International Community documentation.

entries.label: State Shiism's Institutions
entries.hint: The Islamic Republic built an extensive state-clerical infrastructure around Qom's seminaries, though notably Khamenei's own religious scholarly credentials as a marja (source of emulation) were and remain contested by some senior ayatollahs — a tension between formal political authority and traditional religious scholarly hierarchy that predates, and has outlasted, his decades in office.
entries.note: Comparative accounts of clerical debate over Khamenei's marja status following his 1989 elevation.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Two Academy Awards for Iranian cinema, and the visual culture of protest

entries.label: Two Academy Awards for Iranian Cinema
entries.hint: Asghar Farhadi's A Separation (2011) and The Salesman (2016) won the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film in 2012 and 2017 respectively, continuing a tradition of internationally acclaimed Iranian filmmaking — from Abbas Kiarostami onward — that has persisted throughout the Islamic Republic's history despite operating under strict state content and production restrictions.
entries.note: Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences awards records, 2012 and 2017.

entries.label: The Visual Culture of Woman, Life, Freedom
entries.hint: The 2022–23 protest movement generated a distinctive visual and slogan culture — cut hair as a symbol of defiance, murals and street art quickly painted over by authorities and repainted elsewhere, the Kurdish-origin chant 'Jin, Jiyan, Azadi' (Woman, Life, Freedom) translated into Persian and adopted nationwide — documented extensively through social media given the constraints on domestic and foreign press access.
entries.note: Comparative documentation of 2022–23 protest visual and slogan culture via social media and diaspora media archives.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Reformist religious philosophy under state pressure

entries.label: Soroush's Reformist Religious Philosophy
entries.hint: Philosopher Abdolkarim Soroush argued that religious knowledge itself is historically contingent and subject to reinterpretation — a challenge to claims of fixed clerical authority over religious truth that made him an influential reformist intellectual figure and, eventually, a target of state pressure that led him to leave Iran.
entries.note: Abdolkarim Soroush, The Expansion of Prophetic Experience and other collected essays, 1990s–2000s.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: Decades of sanctions and a state still dependent on oil

entries.label: Continued Oil Revenue Dependency
entries.hint: Despite decades of stated government policy aiming to diversify the economy away from oil dependency, hydrocarbon exports have remained the dominant source of foreign currency earnings and a major share of government budget revenue throughout the Islamic Republic's history, leaving state finances persistently exposed to global oil price swings and sanctions-driven export restrictions alike.
entries.note: Central Bank of Iran and OPEC statistical data on Iranian oil export revenue as a share of GDP and government budget, various years.

entries.label: Decades of International Sanctions
entries.hint: US and later broader international sanctions, imposed and expanded in stages since the 1979 hostage crisis and intensified over the nuclear programme, have restricted Iran's oil exports, banking access and imported technology for most of the Islamic Republic's history — Iranian officials attribute much of the country's economic hardship to sanctions, while sanctioning governments and some independent economists point also to domestic mismanagement and corruption as contributing causes.
entries.note: US Treasury Office of Foreign Assets Control sanctions records; comparative economic analyses attributing varying weight to sanctions versus domestic factors.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The nuclear programme, Natanz, and the Stuxnet cyberattack

entries.label: The Nuclear Programme and Natanz
entries.hint: Iran's uranium enrichment facility at Natanz became the focal point of a decades-long international dispute over whether the country's nuclear programme was purely civilian, as Iranian officials have consistently stated, or intended to develop weapons capability, as Western governments and the International Atomic Energy Agency have at various points expressed concern about based on inspection findings.
entries.note: International Atomic Energy Agency inspection reports on Natanz, various years; comparative Iranian and Western government statements on the programme's aims.

entries.label: The Stuxnet Cyberattack
entries.hint: A sophisticated computer worm, later widely attributed by independent security researchers and, according to subsequent reporting, acknowledged informally by American and Israeli officials, physically damaged centrifuges at Natanz by manipulating their industrial control systems — one of the first publicly documented cyberattacks to cause deliberate physical infrastructure damage rather than only stealing or corrupting data.
entries.note: Symantec, 'W32.Stuxnet Dossier' (2011), the primary independent technical analysis of the worm.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: The 2015 nuclear deal and its unilateral unwinding

entries.label: The Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action
entries.hint: Iran and six world powers (the US, UK, France, Russia, China and Germany) reached a 2015 agreement lifting most international sanctions in exchange for verified restrictions and enhanced inspection of Iran's nuclear programme — a landmark diplomatic settlement that the International Atomic Energy Agency subsequently certified Iran was complying with.
entries.note: Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (2015), full text; IAEA compliance verification reports, 2016–2018.

entries.label: The US Withdrawal from the Nuclear Deal
entries.hint: The United States unilaterally withdrew from the 2015 nuclear agreement in 2018 and reimposed sanctions despite the IAEA's certification of Iranian compliance and the objections of the other signatory powers — a decision after which Iran progressively reduced its own compliance with the agreement's technical restrictions in the years that followed.
entries.note: US State Department withdrawal announcement (2018); IAEA reports on Iranian compliance reductions following the US withdrawal.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: A regional network of allied and aligned armed groups

entries.label: A Regional Network of Allied Armed Groups
entries.hint: Since founding and funding Lebanon's Hezbollah in 1982, Iran has built relationships of varying closeness with armed groups and political movements across Iraq, Syria, Yemen and the Palestinian territories often described collectively as an 'axis of resistance' — a network Iranian officials describe as solidarity with allied causes and regional deterrence, while opposing governments describe it as regional destabilisation and proxy warfare.
entries.note: Comparative regional-security analysis of Iran's relationships with allied and aligned non-state armed groups, with the customary caution that Iranian and opposing-government framings of this network differ substantially.

entries.label: The Rivalry with Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: Shia Iran and Sunni Saudi Arabia have competed for regional influence since 1979 along lines that are simultaneously sectarian, geopolitical and economic — a rivalry that has played out through proxy conflicts, oil-market competition and periodic direct diplomatic ruptures and, at other points, tentative rapprochement efforts.
entries.note: Comparative Iran-Saudi diplomatic relations history, 1979–2026.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: The mandatory hijab, a death in custody, and documented minority persecution

entries.label: Criminalization under the Islamic Penal Code
entries.hint: Iran's Islamic Penal Code criminalises consensual same-sex sexual acts between adults, with penalties that include the death penalty for certain specified acts — among the most severe legal frameworks of its kind still in active use anywhere in the world, documented directly in the legal code itself rather than only in advocacy reporting about its enforcement.
entries.note: Islamic Penal Code of Iran (1991, revised 2013), Articles on same-sex sexual acts.

entries.label: The Mandatory Hijab and Mahsa Amini's Death
entries.hint: Mandatory hijab in public, legally required since 1983, has been enforced with varying intensity by police and, since the 2000s, a dedicated 'morality police' unit — Mahsa Jina Amini's death in that unit's custody in September 2022 became the immediate catalyst for the largest women's-rights-centred protest movement in the Islamic Republic's history, discussed further under Conflict.
entries.note: Islamic Penal Code provisions on hijab enforcement; coroner and government statements on Mahsa Amini's death, disputed by her family and independent investigators.
